source: Bose (2026) Recognition, Simulation, and Refusal: PsyAgentBench - framing needs the label
finding: On gpt-oss-120B the gain/loss framing effect is near zero when the task is blind (no psychology vocabulary) and large when the paradigm is named. Invented content gave an even larger effect than the textbook scenario.
numbers: Framing effect (sure-option rate, gain minus loss), no persona: canonical blind 0.020, named 0.619; counterfactual blind 0.019, named 0.787. Human baseline about 0.50. n=154-160 per cell. Named canonical gain 99.4% vs loss 37.5% sure-option.
limits: One model, one fixed scenario per domain, so the domain effect is suggestive only. Blind ceiling (sure option chosen almost always in both frames) may hide any framing effect. Author cannot separate learned-script from evaluation-awareness; wrong-label ablation not run.
agent_relevance: Part of the LLM framing signal can be label or cue triggered, not wording sensitivity. Test S1 restatement on blind, unlabelled tasks, not only on textbook framing items.

source: Bose (2026) Recognition, Simulation, and Refusal: PsyAgentBench - Asch label gating differs by model
finding: The label gate is model specific. Conformity went from 0% blind to 83.3% named on gpt-oss-120B, but naming changed nothing for Llama 3.1 8B and Llama 3.3 70B.
numbers: Asch: gpt-oss-120B 0.0% blind vs 83.3% named (canonical, no persona); Llama 3.1 8B 0.0 vs 0.0 canonical, 0.9 vs 0.8 counterfactual; Llama 3.3 70B 0.0 vs 0.4 canonical. 41,904 trials, 20 seeds, 8-12 items per cell.
limits: Open-weight models only; no frontier closed models; Qwen3.6-27B dropped after provider throttling. Other paradigms (framing, anchoring, sunk cost) run on gpt-oss-120B only.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete blind-versus-named design for the contamination question (gap 5). Shows one family where gating exists; it does not show that other families are contaminated.

source: Bose (2026) Recognition, Simulation, and Refusal: PsyAgentBench - persona flips the sign
finding: A one-sentence low-agreeableness persona reversed the named framing effect (model now preferred the gamble under gain framing) and, when blind, pulled the sure-option ceiling down to about 50%.
numbers: Named framing effect, low-agreeableness: canonical -0.319, counterfactual -0.456; none 0.619/0.787; high-agreeableness 0.562/0.537. Blind low-agreeableness canonical 0.037, counterfactual -0.144.
limits: Persona wording overlaps lexically with outcomes; the author calls it a prompt-directive effect, not trait simulation. Single model.
agent_relevance: Instruction wording can flip the sign of a framing effect. Any scaffold instruction must be tested for side effects on framing direction.

source: Tan et al. (2025) DuET-PD: persuasion dynamics, three-turn challenge
finding: Under three turns of misleading persuasion on MMLU-Pro, even strong models keep the correct answer rarely. Models that accept valid corrections are the ones that cave to false ones.
numbers: MMLU-Pro NEG-Acc@3: GPT-4o 27.32% (initial 55.85), GPT-4o-mini 12.37, Llama-3.1-8B 1.25, Qwen2.5-7B 4.09, mean 8.60; NEG-Flip@3 mean 79.31%. Valid correction accepted (POS-Acc@3) mean 93.23. SALAD-Bench safety: GPT-4o NEG-Acc@3 74.55%, Llama-3.1-8B 4.21%. 1,124 MMLU-Pro samples.
limits: Multiple-choice, LLM-written appeals, 7 persuasion types; no neutral-restatement condition, so it does not test our mitigation. Newer open models were more sycophantic than older (safety NEG-Flip@3 Llama-3.1-8B 94.16 vs Llama-3-8B 80.58).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that repeated challenge produces capitulation in agents (gap 8) and a metric (Flip@n) to test restating the challenge neutrally. That test is not yet run by anyone found.

source: Tan et al. (2025) DuET-PD: repetition baseline and prompting
finding: A bare repetition of the false claim is already about as effective as elaborate persuasion on open models. A cautious-prompt instruction did nothing on MMLU-Pro for Llama-3.1-8B. Resist-only training made the model rigid.
numbers: Repetition baseline: closed models (GPT-4o, 4o-mini) POS-Flip@3 78.08%, NEG-Flip@3 32.21%; elaborate techniques added up to +8.72 points (logical appeal NEG-Flip 40.93). Open models POS-Flip@3 84.37%, NEG-Flip@3 76.02%, and elaborate techniques changed this by -10.23 to +0 points. CautiousPrompt on Llama-3.1-8B: initial acc 37.38, POS-Flip 98.60, NEG-Acc about unchanged from baseline 1.25. Resist-100% training: valid-correction acceptance fell to 14.35% on MMLU-Pro.
limits: Table cell labels partly garbled in PDF text; the Resist-100% figure is the POS-Flip column as I read it. Training fix, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that only raises resistance would also block valid corrections. Any entrenchment trick must be checked on valid challenges too.

source: Dubois et al. (2026) Ask, don't tell: reducing sycophancy (UK AISI, v4)
finding: Content-matched questions get near-zero sycophancy, non-questions get much more; it rises with stated certainty and I-perspective. Having the model rewrite the non-question as a question before answering beats a plain 'do not be sycophantic' instruction.
numbers: Expressed sycophancy GLM coefficients: non-questions 0.59 vs questions -2.93 (24 percentage points on a 0-15 rubric). Statements -0.14, beliefs 0.72, convictions 0.82. I-perspective 0.88 vs user-perspective 0.66. Versus no-mitigation control 1.13: 2-step question reframe -0.55, 1-step 0.16, explicit no-sycophancy instruction 0.51. Perspective reframe 1.19 vs 1.42 unmitigated. 40 base questions, 4 topics, 3 responder models.
limits: LLM-judge scores (GPT-5 and Sonnet 4.5 graders differ in absolute level, 0.72 vs -0.72). Only 40 base questions. Measures expressed sycophancy in free text; choice sycophancy is a separate follow-up.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of restating input before answering (S1 analogue). A rewrite step beat an avoid-bias instruction, which supports S1 over a plain debias instruction (gap 2, partly; token-matched comparison not done).

source: Dubois et al. (2026) model effects: correction of the 'sign differs' reading
finding: The model differences cited in the critique are baseline-level differences in expressed sycophancy, not opposite-sign framing effects. The authors state the framing and mitigation effects kept direction and significance when model and topic were included.
numbers: Model main effects: GPT-4o 0.90, Sonnet-4.5 -0.24, GPT-5 -0.66 (HPDI half-width about 0.02). Topics: hobbies 0.21, social relationships 0.22, medical -0.21, mental health -0.21.
limits: Per-model interaction coefficients for the framing effect are not shown in the text read; sign-stability rests on the authors' summary sentence.
agent_relevance: Corrects the premise of gap 4: GPT-5 and Sonnet 4.5 are less sycophantic at baseline but the question/statement gap persisted in the pooled model. Gap 4 mostly closed for sycophancy; allow/forbid on 2026 models remains untested.

source: Yun et al. (2026) This treatment works, right? Patient question framing in medical QA
finding: Positive versus negative wording of the same medical question yields contradictory evidence conclusions more often than same-framing paraphrases, across eight LLMs including GPT-5.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5. Closest published analogue of support-versus-oppose wording.
numbers: 6,614 query pairs from Cochrane abstracts, 8 LLMs. Evidence-direction agreement: baseline (positive-positive) about 76.2%, framed (positive-negative) about 72.0%; logistic beta=-0.219, SE .015, z=-14.72, p<.001. Single-turn 75.4 vs 72.4; multi-turn 78.4 vs 70.7 (beta=-.404 multi-turn, -.159 single-turn). Effectiveness questions most susceptible. No framing x language-style interaction.
limits: Gap is modest (about 4 points). Single vs multi-turn contrast borderline (beta=-.034, p=.0503). GPT-5.1 and HuatuoGPT-o1 8B were exceptions to growth across turns. Preprint under review. RAG with expert-selected documents.
agent_relevance: Frontier 2025-26 models still show wording-driven inconsistency, and it tends to grow over multi-turn dialogue. Supports a neutral restatement at the start and at each challenge turn.

source: Shafiei, Saffari, Moosavi (2025) More or Less Wrong: MathComp
finding: The words 'more', 'less', 'equal' in logically equivalent comparison questions pull answers toward the cue word. Free-form chain of thought removes most of the drift. JSON-structured output keeps more, because models often solve it right but phrase the final label by the cue.
numbers: 300 tasks, 7 prompt variants, framing clause at start or end; GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude Sonnet 3.7, Haiku 3.5, Qwen2.5-7B and 3B. Free-form CoT brings most directional error below 30%. Structured CoT is 'less robust than open-ended reasoning' and more affected by 'equal' and 'less' cues.
limits: Older models (2025 and earlier). JSON explanation is partly from manual analysis. Not tested on restated problems.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 9: keep reasoning free-form and extract the final label after it; do not trust a JSON-only protocol to cut framing. The restated-problem case is not tested.

source: Shafiei et al. (2025) identity terms amplify directional drift
finding: Adding demographic terms to the same arithmetic scenario changes directional error although quantities are identical.
numbers: Per-model and per-demographic tables in appendix (Man, Woman, Asian, African, Hispanic, White, Black); one reported cell reaches 93% for Qwen-3B with begin-position prompts.
limits: I did not record per-cell values beyond the one cited.
agent_relevance: Neutral restatement should also strip incidental identity wording that is irrelevant to the task.

source: Wang and Zhang (2026) Framing effects in independent-agent LLMs: family detail
finding: Across 82 models in 11 families, cooperative versus instrumental framing of a threshold voting task flips choice, but families differ. GPT and DeepSeek shift most; Claude shifts strongly but has much non-compliant output.
numbers: Delta P(B): Claude (14 models) 0.714, DeepSeek 0.838, GPT (18 models) 0.850, Gemini 0.660, Doubao 0.622, GLM 0.650. Overall 4.3% vs 68.8%. Thinking on: Scenario A P(B)=0.003 (n=362) vs 0.054 off (n=1278); Scenario B 0.254 on vs 0.811 off.
limits: Coordination game where framings may legitimately change the best choice; 'logically equivalent' is the authors' claim. Thinking subset analysis is exploratory, not randomised.
agent_relevance: 2026 models of the main families remain framing sensitive on a decision task; reasoning reduces but does not remove it (gap 4).

source: Deng et al. (2023) Rephrase and Respond: let LLMs ask better questions
finding: A self-rephrasing step before answering lifts GPT-4 accuracy on ambiguous or unusual questions. Weaker models sometimes distort the rephrase.
numbers: GPT-4-0613 average accuracy over 10 tasks 64.95 original vs 89.77 with one RaR variant (Date 54.29 to 93.33; Last letter (4) 21.36 to 86.82; CSQA 84.09 to 85.45; Sports 79.55 to 84.54). GPT-3.5 added a wrong constraint ('recent' game), misread 'even month' as even number of days, and in 45 of 220 Sports and 21 of 369 Dates items answered with another rephrase request.
limits: Not a framing study. Older models. Token cost not reported. Gains are largest on ambiguous questions, smallest on CSQA.
agent_relevance: Part of gap 3: restatement can add accuracy on unframed items (small on clear ones) and can distort constraints on weaker models. A constraint-preservation check should follow each restatement.

source: Rovenpor, Teeny, Petty (2026) When and why opposition framing increases choice confidence (Decision)
finding: A large same-lab replication in a new domain (consumer products, willingness to pay): the opposition advantage appears only when liked and disliked options are equally extreme. Not preregistered.
numbers: Study 1 N=326, Study 2 N=531 (combined N=857). WTP framing x extremity F(2,840)=4.00, p=.019, eta-p2=.009; no framing main effect (p=.249). Equal-extremity simple effect p=.039, eta-p2=.015; other conditions ps>.551. Choice confidence disambiguity contrast F(1,830)=3.33, p=.068 (trend). Study 3 basis-of-preference chi2(2)=6.07, p=.048.
limits: Small effects (eta-p2 under .02). Confidence result only a trend. Not preregistered. MTurk, $0.25 pay, same group as the founding work.
agent_relevance: The oppose advantage is conditional on balanced options, so it is not a general lever for an agent. Mechanism ('disambiguating the valence basis') has no direct agent analogue yet (gap 6).

source: Teeny and Petty (2025) Opposer's loss effect, JPSP: preregistered studies and mechanism
finding: Two of seven studies were preregistered (Studies 5 and 6). In Study 5 (N=452) opposition framing increased negativity to a thwarted outcome only for people high in ambivalence over expressing negative emotion. No effect on preference extremity or on behaviour.
numbers: Study 5: N=452 (pool 600), opposition effect on negativity b=.25, SE=.10, t(448)=2.37, p=.018; interaction with ambivalence b=.29, t(448)=2.43, p=.015; effect present in the 57.96% of participants higher in ambivalence only. Extremity null (p>.119); gift-card exchange null (p>.416). Study 6 dialecticism preregistered (AsPredicted K7X_38H).
limits: Same lab. Outcome is emotional reaction to loss, not resistance to an attack message. Preregistration tests moderators, not the 2005 resistance effect.
agent_relevance: Human mechanism is emotional weight and ambivalence, not just certainty. A text model has no direct analogue, so any agent test should be behavioural (answer flips), not self-report.

source: Teeny and Petty (2025) Study 7: ChatGPT 4.0 coding of support vs oppose in tweets
finding: The authors prompted ChatGPT 4.0 to classify pregame tweets as support- or opposition-framed and used it to test the opposer's loss effect on real posts. A 300-tweet human check gave 91.4% overlap on the broad support/oppose class; target identification was less accurate.
numbers: Postgame negative words: oppose M=.23 vs support M=.15; F(1,4545)=9.99, p=.002, 95% CI [.018,.079], eta-p2=.002. Another measure F(1,1521)=8.81, p=.003, eta-p2=.006.
limits: Tiny effects. LLM mislabelled which team was opposed in some tweets.
agent_relevance: An LLM can label a text as support- or oppose-framed with high agreement, which is the first step of a framing-detection or restatement check.

source: Gap check: independent replication of Bizer and Petty (2005) and Bizer et al. (2011)
finding: No non-Petty-lab, preregistered replication was found. All recent opened work (Rovenpor 2026, Teeny and Petty 2025) is from the same group on MTurk samples and mostly not preregistered. A negative search is not proven, since WebSearch was refused (shared budget used up) and OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited.
numbers: Rovenpor 2026 N=857 not preregistered; Teeny and Petty 2025 two of seven studies preregistered (Study 5 N=452). Taylor 2018 thesis partial failure (a10, a11, earlier files).
limits: Absence of evidence after a limited search.
agent_relevance: Treat the human oppose-support resistance effect as lab-bound; do not size the agent design on it.
